lead: One process may hold many threads, one machine may hold many cores, and one job may carry a deadline. The scheduler then answers three questions: which thread of the process runs, which CPU runs it, and which deadline is nearest. This chapter links those three levels. You meet them in a phone with eight cores, in a web server with a shared ready queue, and in a car's braking controller where a late answer is a wrong answer.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.5 for threads and Chapter 2.7 for priority and preemption.

blocks.text: A user thread is created by a library. The kernel may not see it. A kernel thread is scheduled by the OS. A light-weight process (LWP) is the kernel-schedulable object that a user thread runs on. The mapping between user threads and LWPs decides who competes with whom.

Contention scope names the competition. In process-contention scope (PCS), user threads compete only inside their own process for one available LWP. The thread library picks the winner. In system-contention scope (SCS), kernel threads compete with all other kernel threads for the CPUs. The kernel picks the winner.

Example: a process has three user threads and two LWPs. Under PCS, the three threads share those two LWPs; the library chooses which two run at a time. Under SCS, the two LWPs sit in the system ready queue beside threads from other processes. A one-to-one model gives every user thread its own LWP, so SCS applies directly. A many-to-one model has many user threads on one LWP, so PCS does the real work.

Asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP) lets one processor run the scheduler and assign work to the others. The others run only assigned threads. Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) lets every processor run the scheduler and take work from a shared or per-CPU ready queue. General-purpose systems use SMP because it scales and has no single scheduling bottleneck.

Load balancing keeps CPUs busy. Push migration has a periodic kernel task move threads from an overloaded CPU to a light CPU. Pull migration has an idle CPU take a thread from a busy CPU's queue. Both need a measure of load: run-queue length is simple; CPU utilization is better but harder to read.

Processor affinity keeps a thread on the same CPU when possible. A warm cache and valid translation look-aside buffer entries make the next run faster. Soft affinity lets the scheduler migrate the thread but tries to avoid it. Hard affinity uses a system call to pin the thread to a set of CPUs. Hard affinity also helps when a thread must stay near its data or device.

sections.h3: Real-time CPU scheduling: meet the deadline

blocks.text: A real-time task has a deadline: the time by which its job must finish. A periodic task releases a job every period p and needs execution time t in each period. Its utilization is t/p.

blocks.where: U is total CPU utilization, from 0 to 1; tᵢ is the execution time of task i per job, in ms; pᵢ is its period, in ms.

blocks.text: Admission control decides whether to accept a new task. It admits the task only if the set can be scheduled. Rejecting a task is better than missing a brake deadline.

Rate-monotonic scheduling (RMS) gives a static priority: shorter period gets higher priority. It is preemptive. A task set with n tasks is guaranteed schedulable if U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1). For n=2 the bound is 0.828; as n grows it tends to 0.693. This is a sufficient test, not a necessary one.

blocks.where: U is total utilization; n is the number of tasks; the bound is 0.828 for n=2 and tends to 0.693 as n grows.

blocks.text: Earliest-deadline-first (EDF) gives a dynamic priority: the job with the nearest absolute deadline runs first. On one CPU, EDF is optimal for preemptive periodic tasks when each deadline equals its period. RMS is simpler and needs no priority change at run time. The trap is to give the shorter-period task the lower priority. Priority goes to the shorter period.

figure.caption: T1 has the shorter period, so it gets higher priority and preempts T2 at 16 ms. Every job finishes before its deadline.

spec.aria: A 20 ms real-time schedule where T1 (period 4 ms, execution 1 ms) preempts T2 (period 5 ms, execution 2 ms) at 16 ms, and every job completes before its deadline.

examples.question: Task T1 has period 4 ms and execution time 1 ms. Task T2 has period 5 ms and execution time 2 ms. Both are released at time 0. Test rate-monotonic schedulability, draw the schedule up to 20 ms, and list completion times against deadlines.
steps: Priorities: T1 period 4 ms is shorter than T2 period 5 ms, so T1 has higher priority.
T1 completions: 1, 5, 9, 13, 17 ms against deadlines 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 ms. T2 completions: 3, 7, 12, 18 ms against deadlines 5, 10, 15, 20 ms. Every completion is before its deadline.
Idle times: 3–4, 7–8, 9–10, 13–15 and 18–20 ms. At 15 ms T2 starts; T1 preempts at 16 ms; T2 resumes at 17 ms and finishes at 18 ms.
examples.answer: U = 0.65 ≤ 0.8284271247461903, so the set passes the rate-monotonic test; T1 has higher priority and no deadline is missed up to 20 ms.
examples.check:
import math
t1,p1=1,4
t2,p2=2,5
U=t1/p1+t2/p2
n=2
bound=n*(2**(1/n)-1)
print(U)
print(bound)

traps: Longer period gets higher rate-monotonic priority. It is the reverse: shorter period, higher priority.
The utilization bound is treated as exact. It is sufficient: a set above the bound may still pass a full schedule check.
PCS and SCS are swapped. PCS is competition inside one process; SCS is competition among kernel threads for CPUs.
Hard and soft affinity are swapped. Soft tries to keep a thread on a CPU; hard pins it.
EDF is called static. EDF priority changes as absolute deadlines approach; RMS priority is static.

quiz.q: Define process-contention scope and system-contention scope.
quiz.a: PCS: user threads compete only inside their own process for an LWP. SCS: kernel threads compete with all kernel threads for the CPUs.

quiz.q: Why does processor affinity improve performance?
quiz.a: A thread that stays on one CPU keeps warm cache lines and valid translation look-aside buffer entries, so its next run has fewer cache and TLB misses.

quiz.q: Task A has t=2 ms and p=5 ms. Task B has t=1 ms and p=10 ms. Compute U. Does the two-task RM bound guarantee schedulability?
A two-task set has U=0.9. Can you conclude that RMS fails?
quiz.a: No. The RM utilization bound is sufficient, not necessary. U=0.9 is above 0.828, so the simple test cannot guarantee success; a full schedule check may still pass. EDF can meet all deadlines if U ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Distinguish push migration from pull migration.
quiz.a: Push migration: a periodic kernel task moves threads from an overloaded CPU to a light CPU. Pull migration: an idle CPU takes a thread from a busy CPU's queue.

quiz.q: At time 0, jobs J1 with deadline 8, J2 with deadline 5, and J3 with deadline 12 are ready. Which does EDF run first?
quiz.a: EDF runs J2 first because its absolute deadline 5 is the nearest.

quiz.q: Why does RMS assign higher priority to a shorter period?
quiz.a: A shorter-period task releases jobs more often, so it has less slack between jobs. A static high priority protects it from a longer-period task that can wait longer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems add mixed-criticality tasks, where some jobs may miss a deadline while others must not. Linux exposes real-time policies such as SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR and SCHED_DEADLINE. Response-time analysis gives a tighter test than the utilization bound. Multiprocessor real-time scheduling must also handle migration and shared caches. Search for rate-monotonic analysis, earliest-deadline-first, and mixed-criticality scheduling.
